sample_os_scheduling.title: Operating Systems: CPU Scheduling & Round Robin Algorithm
sample_os_scheduling.raw_transcript: Good morning everyone. Today we are diving into one of the most critical topics in Operating Systems: CPU Scheduling. The CPU is the brain of the computer, and when multiple processes want to run simultaneously, the OS scheduler must decide which process gets CPU time and for how long. First, let's understand the difference between Preemptive and Non-Preemptive scheduling. In non-preemptive scheduling, once a process gets the CPU, it keeps running until it finishes its CPU burst or switches to an I/O wait state. FCFS (First Come First Serve) is a classic example. But in preemptive scheduling, the operating system can interrupt a currently running process to give the CPU to another higher-priority process. Professor, does preemptive scheduling cause overhead because of context switching? Excellent question. Yes, absolutely. Context switching requires saving the CPU registers, program counter, and stack pointer of the old process and loading the state of the new process. This takes memory bus cycles and CPU time, so too frequent preemption degrades overall throughput. Now let us focus on Round Robin Scheduling, denoted as RR. Round Robin is designed specifically for time-sharing systems. The core concept is the Time Quantum or Time Slice, typically ranging from 10 to 100 milliseconds. The ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The CPU scheduler allocates the CPU to each process for an interval of up to 1 time quantum. What happens if the time quantum expires? If process P1 has a burst time of 24ms and quantum is 4ms, after 4ms a timer interrupt occurs. The OS moves P1 to the tail of the ready queue and dispatches P2. If quantum q is extremely large, Round Robin degrades into First-Come First-Served (FCFS). Conversely, if quantum q is extremely small, say 1 microsecond, context switch overhead dominates and system performance collapses. Rule of thumb for exam questions: You should set the time quantum such that roughly 80 percent of the CPU bursts are shorter than the time quantum. This minimizes context switching while providing excellent response time for interactive processes. Let's calculate average turnaround time: Turnaround time equals Completion time minus Arrival time.

masterclass_os_3hours.title: Complete 3-Hour Masterclass: OS Kernel, CPU Scheduling & Virtual Memory
masterclass_os_3hours.raw_transcript: Welcome everyone to our comprehensive 3-hour masterclass on Operating System internals. Today we will journey through the CPU scheduler, memory virtualization, and deadlock avoidance. Let's begin by defining what a process is. A process is not simply static code on disk; it is an active program in execution with an address space, stack, heap, and register state. At minute 24, let's inspect the Process Control Block, or PCB. The PCB is the central data structure maintained by the kernel for every active task. It contains the Process ID (PID), program counter, CPU registers including general-purpose registers, stack pointer (ESP/RSP), base pointer, and CPU scheduling priority. During a context switch, the OS timer interrupt triggers, switching the CPU from user mode to kernel mode. The kernel saves the outgoing process's hardware register state into its PCB and reloads the incoming process's registers from its PCB before executing IRET. Professor, is context switching purely software or does hardware cache invalidation also play a major role in latency? Brilliant observation! While saving registers to the PCB takes a few dozen clock cycles, the hidden cost of a context switch is the cold CPU cache. When the newly scheduled process starts executing, its instructions and working memory set are not in L1/L2 caches, causing extensive cache misses and memory bus stalls. Now entering Hour 2: CPU Scheduling Algorithms. Let us thoroughly analyze Round Robin (RR) scheduling. The foundational building block of Round Robin is the Time Quantum or Time Slice, typically denoted as q, usually set between 10 to 100 milliseconds. Processes are organized in a circular FIFO queue. Each process executes for at most one time quantum. If the quantum expires before the CPU burst finishes, the hardware timer interrupt fires, preempts the process, and places it at the tail of the ready queue. Consider the mathematical trade-off of time quantum q. If q approaches infinity, Round Robin completely degrades into First-Come First-Served (FCFS), leading to the convoy effect where short interactive processes get stuck waiting behind long batch jobs. Conversely, if q is set extremely small, say 1 microsecond, and context switch overhead takes 0.1 microseconds, then 10% of total CPU time is wasted on context switching overhead rather than doing useful computation! Here is the golden rule of thumb for engineering practice and university exams: You should calibrate the time quantum such that roughly 80 percent of the CPU bursts in your workload are shorter than q. When 80% of bursts complete within their initial quantum, they yield the CPU voluntarily without experiencing preemption, drastically lowering context switch frequency while simultaneously achieving minimal waiting time and fast response time. Welcome to Hour 3 of our masterclass. We begin with Deadlock Prevention and Avoidance. For a deadlock to occur, four Coffman conditions must simultaneously hold true: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. To avoid deadlocks dynamically without rigid static prevention, Edsger Dijkstra formulated the Banker's Algorithm. When a process requests resources, the Banker's algorithm checks whether granting the request leaves the system in a 'Safe State'. A state is safe if there exists an execution sequence P1, P2, ..., Pn such that for each process Pi, the resources that Pi still needs can be satisfied by the currently available resources plus the resources held by all preceding processes. In the final segment of our 3-hour masterclass, let us analyze Virtual Memory and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB). Standard two-level paging requires two memory accesses for every single byte accessed: one to read the Page Directory / Page Table Entry, and a second to access the actual physical data address. This cuts CPU memory speed in half! To solve this, the MMU uses an on-chip hardware associative cache called the TLB. If the virtual page number hits in the TLB, the physical frame address is resolved in less than 1 nanosecond. Effective Memory Access Time is calculated as: EAT = (Hit Ratio * (TLB Time + Memory Time)) + ((1 - Hit Ratio) * (TLB Time + 2 * Memory Time)). With a 98% TLB hit ratio, virtual memory achieves near-native RAM speed.

As a side note, Charles is not just a mathematician or cryptocurrency innovator, but also a Colorado based farmer of bison and mushrooms, a gamer, a fisherman, and a world traveler. When I asked him if he has a nice professional picture of himself, he sent me a picture of him in Mongolia with a hawk on his shoulder, meeting the Mongolian president.
A process is an active program in execution comprising an address space, stack, heap, and register state. The masterclass covers CPU scheduling, memory virtualization, and deadlock avoidance.

The Process Control Block (PCB) is the kernel data structure maintaining PID, program counter, general registers, stack pointer (ESP/RSP), and priority. During a context switch, the kernel saves the outgoing process registers into its PCB and restores the incoming process state. Beyond register copying, the primary hidden cost is cold CPU cache invalidation leading to L1/L2 cache misses.

Round Robin (RR) organizes processes in a circular FIFO queue with a fixed Time Quantum (q, typically 10-100ms). If q approaches infinity, RR degrades into FCFS causing convoy effect. If q is excessively small, context switch overhead dominates CPU cycles and destroys throughput.

The 80% rule of thumb states that 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the time quantum. This ensures most processes terminate or block for I/O voluntarily without preemption, minimizing context switch frequency while preserving interactive responsiveness.

Deadlock requires four simultaneous Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Dijkstra's Banker's Algorithm dynamically avoids deadlock by evaluating if resource allocation leads to a Safe State with a complete safe execution sequence.

Two-level paging doubles memory access latency. The Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) acts as a high-speed hardware cache for page table translations. Effective Memory Access Time (EAT) = (Hit Ratio * (TLB Time + Memory Time)) + ((1 - Hit Ratio) * (TLB Time + 2 * Memory Time)). A 98% hit ratio achieves near-native RAM speed.

Good morning everyone. Today we are diving into one of the most critical topics in Operating Systems: CPU Scheduling. The CPU is the brain of the computer, and when multiple processes want to run simultaneously, the OS scheduler must decide which process gets CPU time and for how long. First, let's understand the difference between Preemptive and Non-Preemptive scheduling. In non-preemptive scheduling, once a process gets the CPU, it keeps running until it finishes its CPU burst or switches to an I/O wait state. FCFS (First Come First Serve) is a classic example. In preemptive scheduling, the operating system can interrupt a currently running process to give the CPU to another higher-priority process. Preemptive scheduling causes overhead due to context switching. Context switching requires saving the CPU registers, program counter, and stack pointer of the old process and loading the state of the new process. This takes memory bus cycles and CPU time, so too frequent preemption degrades overall throughput.

Round Robin Scheduling (RR) is designed specifically for time-sharing systems. The core concept is the Time Quantum or Time Slice, typically ranging from 10 to 100 milliseconds. The ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The CPU scheduler allocates the CPU to each process for an interval of up to 1 time quantum.

What happens if the time quantum expires? If process P1 has a burst time of 24ms and quantum is 4ms, after 4ms a timer interrupt occurs. The OS moves P1 to the tail of the ready queue and dispatches P2. If quantum q is extremely large, Round Robin degrades into First-Come First-Served (FCFS). Conversely, if quantum q is extremely small, say 1 microsecond, context switch overhead dominates and system performance collapses.

Rule of thumb for exam questions: You should set the time quantum such that roughly 80 percent of the CPU bursts are shorter than the time quantum. This minimizes context switching while providing excellent response time for interactive processes. Let's calculate average turnaround time: Turnaround time equals Completion time minus Arrival time.
